title: Mevalonolactone (MVL / mevalonic acid)
headline: A barrier-lipid signal backed by one small, short, double-blind human trial. The louder collagen and hyaluronic-acid claims trace to brand statements, not papers I could find.
evidenceTier: Small human RCT (2 weeks) + cell and 3D-epidermis work; ingredient is a commercial supplier product
fit: Plausible for dry-season barrier support, including on retinoid-treated skin (my inference). Weak fit as an acne or sebum fix: the trial population had dry skin and measured water loss, not breakouts.
displaces: A basic barrier moisturizer. It should replace that step, not add a step.
estimateNote: Prices marked EST are my guesses, not looked up.

cost.label: US
cost.value: US$38 for 1.8 oz (Personal Day Dive Deep Mevalonic Moisturizer, retailer listing)

cost.label: US, budget
cost.value: from about US$21 (Dr. Different 131 Moisturizer, per a third-party aggregator; not label-checked)

cost.label: Canada
cost.value: about C$50-55 if it ships here at a straight currency conversion

buzzCheck: Buzz premium looks modest on price. The real question is dose: no product I found discloses the percentage, and the only human trial used 0.1%.
summaryPoints: Mechanism proposed by the authors: MVL becomes mevalonic acid in water, raises PPAR beta/delta, which raises the lipid transporter ABCA12, which moves free fatty acids into lamellar granules that build the skin's barrier lipids.
In the trial, the placebo group's water loss got worse over 2 winter weeks and the MVL group's did not. The win is protection against deterioration, not improvement from baseline.
Nothing visible should be expected at 2 weeks. The endpoints were instrument readings.

dossier.whatItIs: Mevalonolactone (INCI: Mevalonolactone) is the lactone form of mevalonic acid, a molecule early in the body's cholesterol and isoprenoid pathway. The cosmetic raw material in the trial is produced by fermentation with a sake-related yeast (Saccharomycopsis fibuligera) and sold by ADEKA (Japan) under the name Luminacare. Supplier materials position it as a moisturizing and anti-aging agent.

steps: Applied topically, MVL reverts to mevalonic acid on contact with water (stated in the paper).
In cultured keratinocytes, PPAR beta/delta mRNA rose 1.7-fold and ABCA12 mRNA and protein rose.
ABCA12 is the transporter that loads lipids into lamellar granules, the packets that later become the lipid mortar between skin cells.
Cells showed more and larger lamellar granules, and free fatty acids were higher (myristic acid about 4.6x, palmitic about 3.6x, palmitoleic about 3.3x).
Result claimed: less water loss through the stratum corneum.
mechanism.inferenceFlag: The chain from PPAR to ABCA12 to granules is the authors' inference from cell data. They also argue the effect is unlikely to run through cholesterol, because fatty-acid synthesis enzymes did not change. None of this was shown directly in human skin.
mechanism.diagramCaption: MVL -> mevalonic acid -> PPAR beta/delta up -> ABCA12 up -> lipid loading into lamellar granules -> barrier lipids -> lower water loss (authors' model)

flow.label: Applied at 0.1% in a lotion
flow.note: The human trial used a lotion with 0.1% MVL on the face twice daily for two weeks, against the same lotion without it.

flow.label: Reverts to mevalonic acid in water
flow.note: Stated in the paper as a property of the compound. It is the starting assumption for everything after it.

flow.label: PPAR beta/delta signal up 1.7 times
flow.note: Cultured keratinocytes, not people. PPAR beta/delta mRNA rose 1.7-fold.

flow.label: ABCA12 lipid transporter up
flow.note: ABCA12 mRNA and protein rose. ABCA12 is the transporter that loads lipids into lamellar granules.

flow.label: More lamellar granules and free fatty acids
flow.note: In cells: more and larger granules. Free fatty acids rose (myristic about 4.6x, palmitic about 3.6x, palmitoleic about 3.3x).

flow.label: Stronger barrier lipid layer
flow.note: The authors' inference that the cell changes add up to a stronger barrier lipid layer. Not shown directly in human skin.

flow.label: Less water loss over 2 winter weeks
flow.note: Water loss: the placebo group worsened over the 2 weeks, the MVL group did not change; the between-group difference was significant (p<0.05). The corneometer between-group difference was not.

studies.cite: Chen B, Lu N, Lee K, Ye L, Hasegawa C, Maeda K, et al. Application of mevalonolactone prevents deterioration of epidermal barrier function by accelerating the lamellar granule lipid transport system. Skin Res Technol. 2022;28(6):804-814.
studies.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group. 66 women aged 30-60 enrolled; 30 active and 29 placebo analyzed. Two weeks, January-February 2020. Lotion with 0.1% MVL versus the same lotion without it, applied to the face twice daily.
studies.who: Healthy women with low stratum corneum water, high water loss and low surface lipid. Skin disease (atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, ichthyosis) excluded. Mean age about 45. Skin tone and ethnicity are not reported in the text I read. The study site is not stated in the text either.
results: Water loss (TEWL): the placebo group worsened significantly over the 2 weeks; the MVL group did not change. The between-group difference in change was significant (p<0.05).
Stratum corneum water content (Corneometer): rose within the MVL group (p<0.01) but the difference between groups was not significant.
Surface lipid: no change within either group; the between-group change favored MVL (p<0.05). The authors note the reading mixes sebum and skin-barrier lipids, so the source is unclear.
Lab side: in a 3D epidermis model, TEWL was reported as '27% compared with control' (the wording is ambiguous; check the paper before quoting a number).
studies.effectSize: Numeric means and confidence intervals are in scatter plots (figures 5-6) and not in the text I read. I cannot give a percent improvement.
studies.placebo: The placebo lotion contained the base formula, so a plain moisturizer effect is built into the comparison. The placebo group still got worse, which the authors attribute to winter conditions.
studies.material: Not established. Subjects completed skin questionnaires, but those results are not reported in the text I read. A TEWL difference at 2 weeks is a measurable change; whether it is something you would feel is unknown.
studies.adverse: No adverse events are described in the text I read. Absence of reporting is not evidence of safety.
studies.conflict: Authors declare no conflict of interest. The MVL tested was the ADEKA commercial raw material. I could not confirm author affiliations from what I read.
studies.limits: One trial, 59 analyzed people, 2 weeks, dry-skin population, no skin-tone data, no follow-up after stopping, one season. The authors also doubled the concentration relative to cell work because the stratum corneum limits permeability (their statement).

studies.cite: Scopel M, Abraham WR, Antunes AL, Henriques AT, Macedo AJ. Mevalonolactone: an inhibitor of Staphylococcus epidermidis adherence and biofilm formation. Med Chem. 2014;10(3):246-51.
studies.design: Laboratory antibiofilm and antimicrobial assays on S. epidermidis, including 12 clinical isolates.
results: MVL reduced biofilm formation of S. epidermidis without antibacterial activity against the reference strain; the clinical isolates showed both biofilm inhibition and antimicrobial activity. No effect on gram-negative bacteria.
studies.material: Not applicable. S. epidermidis is also a skin commensal, so whether this helps or harms a skin microbiome is unknown.
studies.limits: Laboratory only. Do not read this as an anti-acne finding.

howToUse: Treat it as a barrier-layer swap: PM, after water-based serums, in the slot where a basic moisturizer would go, then occlusive if you use one.
Do not add it on top of a full routine. If it does not replace a step, skip it.
The trial used a lotion with 0.1% applied twice daily. Use any product as directed; there is no tested dose beyond that.
Interactions with retinoids, acids and vitamin C are untested. Nothing I found says it conflicts, but that is absence of data. Introduce it alone for the first week.

expect.what: Probably nothing visible. Check for stinging or new bumps.
If it works as in the trial, less tightness or flaking during dry weather (my inference; the trial measured instruments, not feelings).
No data. Collagen or hyaluronic-acid changes have not been shown in people.

dossier.contraindications: None reported in the paper's text. Not tested in pregnancy, in people with skin disease, or on retinoid-treated skin. Treat a 'no reports' as unknown.
dossier.sideBenefits: None shown in people. The biofilm result is laboratory-only.
wouldChangeVerdict: A second independent trial, ideally 4-8 weeks
A product that discloses the percentage
Results on retinoid-treated or oily, congestion-prone skin
dossier.transfer: Does the mechanism apply to deeper skin tones? The pathway (lipid transport into lamellar granules) is not tone-specific, so I would expect it to transfer. The trial gives no tone data, so that is inference. For this ingredient the efficacy question and the risk question separate: it is not an irritant or exfoliant class, so post-inflammatory pigment risk is not the concern; the vehicle's richness is.
confidence: Read in full: Chen 2022 (open-access full text).
Not opened live: retailer ingredient list, aggregator pages and the patent text (read through search snippets).
Not verified: author affiliations, the study site, numeric effect sizes, the mouse study cited in the press.

structure.note: Flat 2D drawing generated from the structure string with RDKit. Stereochemistry is left out. The structure string, formula and IUPAC name (4-hydroxy-4-methyloxan-2-one) match the FooDB record; I could not open PubChem.

fitLine: Plausible for dry-season barrier support; weak for acne or sebum.
timeline: Instrument change by 2 weeks; felt change unknown

fitAxes.why: Two-week, double-blind trial in dry-skinned women showed protection against water-loss worsening. No data in deeper skin tones.
Not tested on retinoid-treated skin. Fit with a retinoid routine is my inference only.
No comedogenicity or acne data found. Risk depends mostly on the vehicle's richness, which no product discloses.
The trial ran January to February, and the benefit was preventing winter worsening. Fits the dry months.
